title: Push-streaming DRAM: memory runs the schedule, host stops asking
idea: Invert 'memory is a passive slave waiting for commands': the compiler uploads a static access program (tensor walk, bank interleave, refresh slots) into a tiny sequencer on the HBM base die, which activates banks and pushes data down a unidirectional link in fixed slots; the host keeps only a credit/abort lane, no command/address bus.
why: Removes CA pins and host scheduling logic (~15-25% of PHY pins/power), kills turnaround bubbles and lets the base die slot refresh and row-hammer mitigation into idle windows; ~1.3x effective bandwidth for static AI graphs.

title: Wavelength-addressed banks: color selects the bank, not a decoder
idea: Invert 'addresses are decoded electrically in the periphery': each bank group gets a microring drop filter tuned to its own wavelength on a base-die waveguide bus, so a request on lambda-7 physically reaches only bank 7 and data returns on the same color; bank select becomes optical routing with no global address decode tree.
why: Attacks periphery (~49% of die) and global-wire energy; with comb lasers, 16-32 colors x 32 Gb/s per stack at ~1 pJ/bit vs 3-4 pJ/bit HBM.

title: Thread migration to the memory stack instead of data fetch
idea: Invert 'data moves to the compute': when a warp's next N accesses hit one HBM stack, the GPU ships the warp's register context (~2-8 KB) to a small SIMT island on that stack's base die and runs it there, migrating back when locality ends.
why: Moves kilobytes of state instead of megabytes of operands for pointer-chasing, graph and sparse-embedding kernels; 5-20x less off-stack traffic on those kernels, attacking the 20-25% data-movement share of accelerator power.

title: Clamped unbonded die stacks with inductive coupling and swappable layers
idea: Invert 'stacks are permanently bonded': DRAM dies are stacked with no microbumps or TSVs, held by a spring clamp, talking through on-die inductor coils with power fed through edge contacts; a die that fails burn-in is popped out and replaced before final encapsulation.
why: Attacks the HBM TSV tax and 20-30% stack-yield loss: die-level rework turns a scrapped 12-high stack into a one-die swap, and coil area replaces TSV keep-out area.

title: Bookshelf memory: dies stand on edge in a silicon comb
idea: Invert 'dies stack flat on top of each other': thin DRAM dies are inserted vertically like books into a deep-etched silicon comb, I/O routed to one edge and joined by sidewall metallization to the comb floor; each die's full edge is its beachfront and heat flows in-plane to a top cold plate.
why: No TSVs, no 30 um thinning, no vertical thermal stacking penalty; aims at HBM-class density and bandwidth at near-DDR5 wafer area per bit (removing much of the ~3x HBM area tax).

title: The DRAM wafer is the interposer; logic chiplets sit on it
idea: Invert 'memory sits on a passive interposer beside compute': fabricate an uncut DRAM wafer whose top metal levels double as interposer routing, then hybrid-bond GPU/CPU chiplets face-down onto it so every logic tile has gigabytes directly beneath it.
why: Eliminates the separate silicon interposer and TSV stacks; 1-5 um bond pitch gives ~0.05-0.1 pJ/bit and TB/s per mm2 versus 3-4 pJ/bit HBM, while DRAM redundancy absorbs defects at wafer scale.

title: Top-k memory: base die filters KV cache before the link
idea: Invert 'memory returns what was asked for': for attention, the host sends the query vector to the HBM base die, which scores keys in low precision across the KV pages beneath it and returns only the top-k keys/values at full precision.
why: Long-context decode is KV-bandwidth-bound; returning 5-10% of KV entries cuts link traffic 10-20x and lets longer contexts live in fewer, cheaper stacks.

title: Time-coded analog tensor links instead of binary symbols
idea: Invert 'link symbols are digital bits': for weights and activations each wire carries a pulse whose width/edge timing encodes a 6-8-bit value, generated by a delay line and decoded by a time-to-digital converter, accepting ~1 LSB noise that AI numerics tolerate.
why: One edge pair per value instead of up to 8 bit transitions: 3-5x fewer transitions and lower CV2 on in-package links, targeting <0.5 pJ per bit-equivalent.

title: Clockless self-timed DRAM interface with no PLL or DLL
idea: Invert 'memory is synchronous': replace the DLL/PLL and forwarded clocks with delay-insensitive 1-of-4 handshake signaling between base die and host, so links idle at zero power and run as fast as local voltage and temperature allow.
why: Clock trees and DLLs burn much of DRAM I/O idle power and need retraining; self-timed links take idle I/O power toward zero and drop training latency, ~20-30% interface energy saved at low utilization.

title: Optical broadcast of one weight copy to 64 accelerators
idea: Invert 'each accelerator owns a private copy of the model': one memory pool streams weights once into a passive optical star coupler that splits the same light to 64 GPUs in lockstep; each GPU consumes the broadcast layer by layer and keeps only activations and KV in local HBM.
why: Weight replication is a large share of fleet HBM; broadcasting one copy cuts per-GPU weight capacity need by up to ~64x in data-parallel inference, freeing bits rather than making new ones.

title: Power-and-signal superposed TSVs carry DC plus data
idea: Invert 'power and signal need separate vias': each supply TSV carries DC current with a small AC data signal superimposed, separated on each die by an on-die bias-tee (MIM capacitor plus active current source), so power TSVs double as data lanes.
why: Power/ground TSVs are often over half of HBM's TSV count; merging cuts TSV area and keep-out zones ~30-40%, shrinking the HBM TSV area tax.

title: Socketed HBM stacks on lithographic microspring arrays
idea: Invert 'memory is soldered permanently next to the GPU': HBM stacks press onto lithographic microspring contact arrays (~40 um pitch) on the interposer under a lid clamp, so stacks are tested in place, swapped on failure and reused in the next accelerator generation.
why: Turns HBM from a consumable bound to one GPU into a reusable asset; avoids scrapping a whole module when one stack fails and adds 1-2 extra service lives to each stack.

title: Sense-amp-direct bonding: logic reads subarray stripes without global I/O
idea: Invert 'data must leave through global I/O, serializers and pads': hybrid-bond a logic die so every subarray's local sense-amp stripe has ~1 um-pitch bond pads directly above it and logic consumes row buffers in place.
why: Kills global dataline/serializer energy and much periphery; a full 8 Kb row is usable per activation instead of 64 b, erasing the 128x overfetch waste and approaching ~0.02-0.05 pJ/bit transport.

title: Through-silicon light: vertical optical links across IR-transparent dies
idea: Invert 'vertical connections need metal TSVs': silicon is transparent at 1310 nm, so each thinned die carries small emitters and Ge photodiodes in metal-free windows and data beams straight up the stack, die to die, with no holes drilled.
why: Removes TSV etch/fill, keep-out zones and their 20-30% yield hit; each window carries 10-25 Gb/s so ~100 windows replace ~1000 TSVs.

title: Coolant channels that double as liquid-core waveguides
idea: Invert 'cooling and interconnect are separate systems': microfluidic channels etched between stacked dies are filled with a high-index dielectric coolant so each channel also guides light, carrying memory-logic data while removing heat.
why: Lets memory stack directly on hot logic and adds optical bandwidth with no dedicated waveguide layers; attacks data-movement energy and HBM placement limits.

title: Annular DRAM die with the GPU dropped into its hole
idea: Invert 'memory dies are rectangles with one beachfront edge': plasma-dice a DRAM die with a square hole in its center, drop the GPU die into the hole and bridge all four inner edges with short fan-out wiring.
why: Four inner edges give ~4x beachfront per memory die and uniform ~1 mm wires; ~2x bandwidth per package at lower pJ/bit than one-sided HBM placement.

title: Generative weight seeds expanded on the memory base die
idea: Invert 'needed bytes must be stored and moved verbatim': store weights as a PRNG seed plus a low-rank or quantized residual, and let a base-die engine regenerate the full tensor on demand as it streams to the GPU.
why: If 50-80% of weight information folds into seeds plus residual, DRAM capacity and link traffic for weights drop 2-5x, stretching scarce bits.

title: Charge-recycling bus: stacked voltage domains reuse every transition
idea: Invert 'each bit transition dumps its charge to ground': split the bus into N series-stacked voltage domains so charge discharging a line in domain k charges a line in domain k-1, with a small balancing regulator closing the loop.
why: Cuts I/O CV2 energy roughly by N (2-4x) despite the ~1 V floor, attacking the voltage floor and data-movement energy.

title: Read-mostly asymmetric links: fat downstream lanes, thin upstream lane
idea: Invert 'memory links are symmetric and bidirectional': inference reads 20-100x more than it writes, so build PHYs with unidirectional memory-to-host lanes (no turnaround, simpler drivers and termination) plus a narrow write lane.
why: Removes turnaround penalty and halves transceiver complexity per lane; ~20-30% more usable bandwidth per pin and smaller PHY area.

title: In-package mm-wave radio bus replacing interposer wires
idea: Invert 'chiplets must be wired together': each memory and compute chiplet has 200-300 GHz on-chip antennas, the metal lid forms a closed cavity, and links share the medium by frequency division so any memory reaches any compute die without routing.
why: Eliminates interposer routing congestion and enables broadcast; targets ~1-2 pJ/bit at tens of Gb/s per channel without an interposer.

title: Firmware-defined PHY: one memory stack sold into any standard
idea: Invert 'a DRAM's interface is frozen at tapeout': give the base die a reconfigurable PHY that firmware sets to DDR5, LPDDR5X, wide HBM-like or UCIe/CXL modes, so one stack ships into whichever market is shortest.
why: Inventory fungibility during a 4x price spike: bits flow to the scarcest segment without new tape-outs; fewer mask sets and less SKU risk.

title: Stack-first, test-later: base die remaps around untested dies
idea: Invert 'only known-good dies are stacked': stack lightly tested dies with ~20% spare capacity and let the base die run full BIST after bonding, building a per-subarray remap table that routes around bad rows, banks or whole dies.
why: Removes costly per-die KGD testing and turns HBM's 20-30% stack-yield loss into graceful capacity derating.

title: Significance-aware lanes: MSBs robust, LSBs cheap and noisy
idea: Invert 'all bits deserve the same wire': route sign/exponent/high-mantissa bits over full-swing terminated lanes and low-mantissa bits over ultra-low-swing unterminated lanes run at a bit-error rate AI numerics tolerate.
why: Half or more of tensor bits ride at 3-5x lower energy; ~40% lower interface energy for AI traffic.

title: Deep-trench eDRAM chiplet mosaic from U.S. logic fabs
idea: Invert 'bandwidth must come from dense commodity DRAM': tile 16-32 small deep-trench eDRAM chiplets (IBM-heritage process at GlobalFoundries New York) around the accelerator as a hot tier for activations and KV, packaged in the U.S.
why: Density is ~10x below DRAM, but edge bandwidth and ~0.3-0.5 pJ/bit make it a bandwidth-not-capacity tier, trimming hot-data HBM need 20-40% using domestic fabs that exist today.

title: Rectangular glass panels replace round silicon interposers
idea: Invert 'interposers are cut from round silicon wafers': build large memory-plus-logic interposers on 510x515 mm Corning glass panels with through-glass vias and 2 um redistribution lines at the Absolics plant in Georgia.
why: ~3.7x more area per substrate than a 300 mm wafer with no edge waste, low-loss glass for fast links, an all-U.S. alternative to CoWoS; target 2-3x lower interposer cost per mm2.

title: Printed staircase sidewalls replace TSVs in memory stacks
idea: Invert 'vertical interconnect must be drilled through the die': stack DRAM dies offset like stairs and print fine conductive lines down the exposed steps with U.S.-made aerosol-jet printers (New Mexico), linking each die's edge pads to the base.
why: No TSV etch, fill or keep-out zones and no 30 um thinning; removes much of HBM's ~3x area-per-bit tax using domestic tools.

title: Harvested server DIMMs reborn as U.S.-assembled CXL memory pools
idea: Invert 'memory supply must be freshly fabricated': collect DDR4/DDR5 from retired U.S. hyperscaler servers, test and bin in U.S. plants, and remount on CXL expander cards with a domestic controller as a warm tier behind HBM.
why: Millions of GB retire yearly; reuse adds usable supply at near-zero wafer cost while new DRAM is 4x pricier, at ~$1-2/GB refurbishment cost.

title: Disk-drive head wafer fabs pattern fine-pitch memory interposers
idea: Invert 'interposers must come from semiconductor foundries': repurpose recording-head wafer fabs in Minnesota, which already pattern sub-100 nm thin-film features, to make redistribution layers and fine-pitch interposers for memory stacks.
why: Taps idle U.S. thin-film lithography outside the congested CoWoS chain; relief for HBM integration with near-zero new fab capital.

title: Packaging inside the DRAM fab: wafers never leave the building
idea: Invert 'packaging is a separate offshore back end': run wafer-to-wafer hybrid bonding of DRAM array wafers to base-logic wafers inside the U.S. DRAM fab (Idaho/New York) using its cleanroom, metrology and yield data.
why: Removes Asia OSAT round trips, cuts weeks of cycle time and unifies front/back-end yield learning; U.S. HBM-class memory becomes a single-site product.

title: SiGe bipolar PHY chiplets deliver fast I/O from mature U.S. fabs
idea: Invert 'fast memory I/O needs leading-edge CMOS': build the memory SerDes/PHY as a separate chiplet in U.S. SiGe BiCMOS (GlobalFoundries Vermont/New York) whose HBTs exceed 300 GHz fT, while DRAM base logic stays on a mature node.
why: 64-112 Gb/s lanes without foreign leading-edge nodes; cheaper base dies and domestic I/O supply.

title: Active interposer swallows DRAM periphery; arrays go periphery-light
idea: Invert 'periphery lives on the memory die': make the interposer in a U.S. 65-90 nm fab carrying upper decoder levels, refresh control, ECC and repeaters, while hybrid-bonded DRAM dies keep only sense amps and local drivers.
why: Periphery is ~49% of die; moving half onto cheap mature silicon lifts array efficiency toward 70-75%, ~1.4x bits per DRAM wafer.

title: Anodized-aluminum substrates with copper-filled pores replace ABF film
idea: Invert 'package dielectric must be polymer build-up film': anodize thick U.S. aluminum sheet into porous alumina whose self-ordered vertical pores are electroplated with copper to form dense vias, then pattern RDL on top.
why: Drops dependence on single-source Japanese ABF; self-forming via fields give ~1e8 vias/cm2, better thermal conduction and closer CTE match to silicon.

title: DRAM die as the bridge between compute chiplets
idea: Invert 'bridges are just wires': embed a DRAM die as the EMIB-style bridge between two U.S.-fabbed logic dies (Intel Arizona/New Mexico packaging, U.S.-made DRAM), so the die carrying die-to-die wires also stores what they exchange.
why: Memory sits on the communication path; inter-chiplet buffers and KV need no HBM round trip, ~0.1-0.3 pJ/bit and fewer HBM bits spent on staging.

title: MEMS-mirror optical switches rewire memory pools per job
idea: Invert 'memory-to-compute wiring is fixed at build time': use U.S. micromirror fabs (Dallas DLP heritage) to build optical circuit switches that reassign fiber links from memory sleds to accelerators per job within milliseconds.
why: Fixed configurations strand 20-40% of fleet DRAM; reconfigurable pooling raises utilization so fewer bits must be bought.

title: Acoustic through-die links from U.S. FBAR piezo transducers
idea: Invert 'vertical data must flow as electrons': place AlN/ScAlN thin-film bulk-acoustic transducers (made in a Colorado FBAR fab) on each die and send GHz acoustic pulses straight through bonded silicon to a receiver on the next die.
why: No TSVs, holes or optics; ~50 um transducers at ~1-5 Gb/s each let stacks skip the TSV tax with a fully domestic supply chain.

title: Molybdenum TSVs: CTE-matched vias from Colorado ore
idea: Invert 'TSVs are copper and contacts tungsten': fill TSVs with CVD/ALD molybdenum mined and refined in the U.S. (Colorado), whose CTE (~4.8 ppm/K vs ~17 for Cu) sits close to silicon's 2.6.
why: Shrinks TSV stress keep-out zones several-fold for denser TSVs and a smaller HBM area penalty, while avoiding the ~80% China tungsten chokepoint.

title: Diamond interlayers let DRAM sit directly on the hot GPU
idea: Invert 'memory must sit beside the hot compute die': bond thin single-crystal diamond plates grown in Washington state between GPU and stacked DRAM to spread heat sideways, with through-diamond vias carrying signals.
why: Diamond's ~2000 W/m-K lets memory go on top of logic without overheating: face-to-face 3D bandwidth at ~0.1 pJ/bit and no interposer.

title: Backside-powered base die frees the whole front for signals
idea: Invert 'power and signals share the same face': build the HBM base die on a U.S. backside-power process (Intel 18A PowerVia, Arizona) so power enters from the back and every front-side bond carries data.
why: Signal bond density roughly doubles, ~2x I/O per base die, with cleaner power delivery for faster stacks.

title: Tin-free joints: sintered copper bonds from domestic copper
idea: Invert 'packages need tin-silver solder': join dies and stacks with sintered copper-nanoparticle paste or direct Cu-Cu thermocompression, using U.S.-mined copper and no tin, silver or indium.
why: The U.S. mines no tin; copper joints remove that import, conduct better, tolerate higher temperatures and reach finer pitch (<20 um) than solder microbumps.

title: Fluidic self-assembly drops keyed chiplets into substrate wells
idea: Invert 'chiplets must be placed by precision bonders': give memory and logic chiplets unique keyed shapes that settle into matching wells of a glass carrier in a liquid bath, with surface tension giving final alignment before batch bonding.
why: Removes dependence on imported high-precision bonders, assembling thousands of chiplets per minute on a low-capital U.S. line.

title: Adaptive patterning wires each module to measured die positions
idea: Invert 'wiring masks are fixed before chips are placed': place DRAM and logic dies loosely, measure each die's true position and write custom redistribution per package with maskless lithography (Arizona adaptive-patterning lines).
why: Cheap placement plus maskless wiring gives fine-pitch memory links without CoWoS-class bonders or masks; lower capital per unit and an all-U.S. flow.

title: Flex-wrapped memory: DRAM ribbons folded around the compute package
idea: Invert 'memory sits on a flat plane next to compute': mount thinned DRAM dies on U.S.-made polyimide (Ohio) flex with fine-line wiring and fold it around the four sides and top of the accelerator module.
why: Uses five faces instead of one plane: ~3-4x memory contact perimeter and shorter links than 2.5D in the same footprint.

title: Photonic base die: stacks talk to GPUs by fiber
idea: Invert 'the HBM base die is electrical logic beside the GPU': build the base die on a U.S. monolithic silicon-photonics process (GlobalFoundries Fotonix, New York) so all stack I/O leaves as light on fiber and stacks can sit centimeters to meters away.
why: Removes the silicon interposer and its reticle limit on stacks per GPU; ~1-2 pJ/bit with capacity scaling past 8 stacks.

title: Royalty-free wide-slow memory interface for mature U.S. nodes
idea: Invert 'memory interfaces are written by incumbents for leading-edge PHYs': publish a federally sponsored open spec for a 2048-bit, ~2 Gb/s-per-pin unterminated memory interface that any U.S. 28-90 nm fab and glass/organic packager can build.
why: Lowers entry barriers for new U.S. memory makers and packagers; wide-slow short-reach links are cheaper and ~0.5 pJ/bit.

title: Liquid-nitrogen memory vault on U.S. industrial gas
idea: Invert 'memory runs at room temperature beside compute': put DRAM sleds in a liquid-nitrogen bath from domestic air-separation plants next to the racks, linked optically; at 77 K leakage falls orders of magnitude and wire resistance ~5-7x.
why: Refresh nearly vanishes (16-33% of idle power), retention rises, and cold copper allows longer passive links at the same pJ/bit.

title: Interference-lithography buses: the memory bus is a grating
idea: Invert 'interconnect needs mask-based photolithography': memory buses are thousands of identical parallel lines, so pattern them with maskless two-beam laser interference lithography (U.S.-buildable tool), then cut and connect line ends with coarse lithography.
why: Sub-micron bus pitch on interposers without masks or scanners; very low capital and fully U.S. tooling.
